title: Distant earthquake count ratios were lower at 0-6 than at 6-24 hours after 125 M7.5+ ComCat events in 2001-2024
abstract: We tested whether the after-to-before catalog count ratio differed between early and later hours after large earthquakes. We used 12,848 global M5.5+ ComCat events from a fixed 2000-2025 snapshot. Centers were 125 M7.5+ events in 2001-2024. At surface distances above 1000 km, the first six hours had 27 after and 63 before counts. The 6-24 hour windows had 119 after and 108 before counts. The ratio of these two ratios was 0.389. Its conditional 95% year-resampling interval was 0.224-0.610. A shared within-year time-shift test of the early-minus-later after share gave a lower-tail p value of 0.0026. Two-year blocks, other distance limits and a center isolation filter kept the contrast. The M6+ interval depended on the resampling choice. This formal timing contrast extends prior campaign counts on the same data. It is not independent confirmation. It supports a short early catalog deficit relative to later hours. It cannot show physical recovery, missed detections or an exact recovery time. Mixed magnitudes, dependent events, catalog revisions and the shift assumption limit inference. Code, source hashes, aggregate results, simulation draws, an audit and a figure are included. External event records remain outside the bundle.

display.caption: Left: after-to-before count ratios with conditional 95% year-resampling intervals. Right: early-minus-later after-share contrast under shared within-year time shifts. Counts are event-center incidences.

citations.reason: Its early and later aggregate counts motivate this formal timing contrast. Same source and centers; not independent replication.
